title: Raga Prabhati
hook: the Granth turns from evening to daybreak, and Guru Nanak's first Prabhati hymn names what to put on before anything else

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Kalyan, with Guru Arjan's bee that comes back to the lotus again and again. Your line was evening peace. What did you come back to last night? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

What's the first thing you put on in the morning? Glasses, maybe. A watch. A ring that's been on the nightstand. A wristband. A turban, tied fresh, fold by fold, before the house is awake. Whatever it is, it goes on before the day can ask anything of you, and it says something about who walks out the door. For two days the Granth has been in the evening. Now it turns a page and the sky is getting light. The raga is Prabhati, and tradition sings it at dawn. And Guru Nanak opens it with something to wear.
screen: `WHAT GOES ON FIRST?` → `EVENING TURNS TO DAYBREAK.` → `A HYMN ABOUT WHAT TO WEAR.`

segments.voice: Where we are: in the Granth's order, Prabhati follows Kalyan. Hymns of Gurus open it, and then come Bhagats whose words the Gurus set beside their own, Kabir among them; tomorrow we'll read one of his. Tradition sings Prabhati in the early morning, at the edge of light. Teachers describe the moods of ragas differently, so take the timing as tradition, not as a rule in the text. The text is Guru Nanak's opening hymn. In paraphrase: by your Name we cross over. Your Name is honor, and it is worship. Your Name is my ornament, and the aim of my understanding. Without the Name, there is never honor. Then the center line, the Rahao: all other cleverness is only show; whoever you forgive, their work is made complete. A piece of jewelry is the thing you put on so it's seen, the finishing touch. Guru Nanak takes that word and gives it to the Name. So in the dawn raga, the first thing to put on isn't a watch or a ring. It's remembering. Sikhs speak of the hours before dawn as amrit vela, the ambrosial time, and in the Japji, Guru Nanak links that early hour with the true Name and reflection on greatness. Prabhati sings into that same hour. Now hear the Rahao in the morning. All other cleverness is only show. The early hours are when the mind starts planning: what to say, how to win, how to look. The hymn doesn't throw planning away. It puts it second. First the Name, the ornament. Then the day. Today's line is one word: dawn.
screen: `PRABHATI FOLLOWS KALYAN.` · `TRADITION: SUNG AT DAYBREAK.` · `YOUR NAME IS MY ORNAMENT.` · `ALL OTHER CLEVERNESS IS SHOW.` · then, large: `DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen at dawn. If you can, tomorrow morning, before the phone, play a shabad sung in Raga Prabhati. For now, sit as if it were early: the house quiet, the light thin. Let the breath be slow and even. Before any plan for the day takes shape, let the first thing you put on be something other than a plan. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be that ornament, said once, slowly, on the breath. If you don't, let it be a minute of simple attention, worn before anything else. When the clever thoughts start arriving, let them wait at the door. The bell holds the time.
Raga Prabhati. The raga that follows Kalyan, which tradition sings at daybreak, opening with Guru Nanak's hymn: your Name is my ornament, and all other cleverness is only show. Today's word.
Your line: dawn. Tomorrow morning, before you check anything, take one quiet minute first, and let that be the first thing you wear. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Sikh practice treasures the early hours, amrit vela, for reciting Gurbani; in some gurdwaras the morning kirtan includes shabads sung in Raga Prabhati.
